passage:
In the modern digital economy, remote work and flexible working arrangements have transformed traditional workplace structures across the globe. Driven by advancements in cloud computing, high-speed internet, and collaborative communication software, many companies have transitioned toward hybrid or fully remote operational models. This shift offers significant benefits to both employers and employees, though it also introduces complex operational and psychological challenges.

One of the main advantages of remote work is the enhanced flexibility it grants to workers. Employees no longer face lengthy daily commutes, allowing them to better balance professional responsibilities with family life and personal commitments. Furthermore, organizations can recruit talented individuals from anywhere in the world without being restricted by geographical boundaries. Studies also indicate that operating remotely can lead to higher job satisfaction and reduced overhead costs for businesses, as companies require smaller physical office spaces.

However, working remotely is not without significant drawbacks. A major concern is the blurring of boundaries between professional obligations and personal life. Without a physical workplace, many employees feel compelled to answer emails and complete tasks outside regular working hours, leading to emotional exhaustion and burnout. Additionally, remote environments can hinder spontaneous collaboration and diminish company culture. Employees may experience feelings of isolation and disconnect from their colleagues, which can negatively affect teamwork and organizational loyalty.

To mitigate these drawbacks, forward-thinking organizations are implementing proactive workplace strategies. Companies are establishing clear rules regarding digital communication, encouraging employees to disconnect completely after working hours. Furthermore, regular virtual team-building activities and occasional in-person gatherings are organized to maintain strong interpersonal connections. By promoting a healthy work-life balance and providing adequate technological support, businesses can foster a productive and sustainable remote workforce.

sectionDesc: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C, or D to indicate the correct answer to each of the questions from 11 to 20.
passage:
Plastic pollution has reached critical levels in global oceans, posing a grave threat to marine biodiversity, coastal economies, and human health. Millions of tons of synthetic plastic waste enter marine ecosystems annually through rivers, improper land-based waste disposal, and commercial shipping activities. Because conventional plastics are non-biodegradable, they persist in the marine environment for centuries, gradually fragmenting into toxic microscopic particles known as microplastics.

Microplastics, defined as plastic particles smaller than five millimeters in diameter, present a unique ecological hazard. Marine organisms—ranging from tiny zooplankton and shellfish to large whales—frequently mistake microplastics for food. Ingestion of these non-nutritive particles can cause physical blockages in internal organs, malnutrition, and chemical toxicity, as plastics readily absorb persistent organic pollutants from surrounding seawater. Consequently, toxic substances bioaccumulate up the marine food chain, eventually posing health risks to humans who consume seafood.

Addressing this pervasive environmental crisis requires coordinated international action and innovative waste management infrastructure. Many coastal nations are enacting strict regulatory bans on single-use plastics, such as plastic straws, carrier bags, and microbeads in cosmetic products. Simultaneously, scientific researchers are pioneering circular economy solutions, including the development of biodegradable bioplastics derived from seaweed and plant polymers. These eco-friendly materials break down naturally in ocean water without leaving harmful chemical residues.

In addition to regulatory bans and material innovations, ocean cleanup technologies are being deployed worldwide. Advanced floating barrier systems designed to intercept riverine plastic before it reaches open seas have shown promising results in major Asian river estuaries. Furthermore, community-led beach cleanup initiatives help raise public awareness regarding consumer waste reduction and proper recycling habits.

Despite these promising advancements, achieving a long-term solution requires continuous global collaboration and financial investment. Developing economies often lack the capital necessary to construct modern municipal recycling plants. Therefore, international financial institutions and developed nations must provide technical assistance and funding to help vulnerable regions build sustainable waste infrastructure. Only through a comprehensive approach combining legislation, technological innovation, and public engagement can global marine environments be effectively preserved.
